name: Students With Disabilities and English Learners
title: Students With Disabilities and English Learners
answer: AI practice tools can give students with disabilities and English learners the repetition, pacing and language support they need to reach the same mathematics. The individualized education program team decides how a tool fits each student's goals, and results for these groups must be checked separately in any pilot. The point is to open access to the math, not to replace the skill the lesson is building.

sections.body: Some students need more repetition or a different pace than a single lesson can provide, and AI practice tools can supply that. For students with disabilities, this often means adaptive practice that slows down, repeats a step, or offers a visual model when a student struggles. For English learners, the barrier is frequently the word problem itself rather than the mathematics inside it. The idea solves the problem of students being blocked from practicing a skill they could otherwise handle, whether by pace or by language. The individualized education program team decides how the tool fits each student's goals.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In mathematics across kindergarten through twelfth grade, a teacher can use an approved tool to produce versions of the same word problem with simpler sentence structure, key terms defined, and a picture where it helps. The math stays exactly the same, so the student practices the skill without being blocked by the language, and over time the teacher raises the language demand as the student's English grows. Read aloud support helps as well, and a student who struggles with reading can have word problems read aloud by a tool such as Microsoft Immersive Reader and focus on the math. The question is always which skill the lesson is building, and in a math lesson reading support usually opens access rather than skipping needed practice. For students with disabilities, adaptive practice can slow down, repeat a step, or offer a visual model when a student struggles.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this evidence as a review of 29 studies of AI with students with disabilities, which found a medium sized positive effect across subjects (Zhang, 2024). No other study, figure or finding is given for this idea.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: Results for students with disabilities and English learners should be watched closely in any pilot, because an average gain across a class can hide a group that is falling behind. Teachers should look separately at how these two groups are doing on checks without the tool. If a tool helps most students but not these groups, it needs adjustment before it spreads. The individualized education program team decides how the tool fits each student's goals, and the teacher decides which skill the lesson is building and when to raise language demand. These decisions stay with people, not with the tool.
